entries.answer_en: I am an AI & Software Engineer with over 15 years of experience across software development, systems, AI, and technical project delivery. I started my career in software and payment systems, managing Kiosk and POS projects in Kuwait. Later, I moved into AI and intelligent automation, working on NLP, speech recognition, and machine learning for educational organizations. Currently, I work at the Ministry of Education in Jordan, where I build LLM, RAG, and Agentic AI solutions for BTEC educational processes, including student assessment support, automated feedback, and exam generation. I hold a B.Sc. in Computer Engineering, a Higher Diploma in Educational Administration, and certifications like PMP and PRINCE2. I am passionate about applying AI to solve real-world problems, especially in education.
entries.followup_en: The Ministry work started in 2023. That is where LLM, RAG, and the question-generation flow live. Production orchestration is Python. LangChain was only a proof of concept, and LangGraph is not in production. At Al Najat from 2017 to 2023 I built a Whisper kiosk, student early-warning with Pandas and sklearn, and helpdesk classification with TF-IDF. From 2010 to 2017 at VNC I managed KNET payment kiosks and POS. I am PMP certified.

entries.answer_en: BTEC is a vocational program in Jordanian schools under the Ministry of Education. Students finish units and assignments. Teachers mark them against learning outcomes. My job is the software around that: admin systems, plus AI tools that help teachers with questions, feedback, and review.
entries.followup_en: A unit has content and learning outcomes. Questions and feedback must stay inside that content, not general internet knowledge. That is why generation uses retrieval first. Teachers still own the mark and the question bank. The software helps them move faster. It does not replace assessment.

entries.answer_en: This is the LLM project at the Ministry. I retrieve the BTEC unit text and learning outcomes, and the model writes questions and feedback only from that text. Output is JSON, checked with Pydantic. A teacher must approve before anything is saved, and I wrote that flow in Python.
entries.followup_en: I did not send one giant prompt. Retrieval, generation, schema check, then a pause. That is agentic in the practical sense: a goal, tools, state between steps, and a stop for a person. LangChain helped the proof of concept. LangGraph would fit the pause and checkpoints, but it is not what runs today. Student names never go to the model. Curriculum text does.
entries.answer_ar: النظام يجلب محتوى الوحدة أولاً، ثم يولّد أسئلة منها فقط بشكل JSON، ولا يحفظ شيئاً إلا بعد موافقة المعلم.

aliases: why did you split question generation into steps

entries.answer_en: Because one giant prompt gives me output I cannot check. First, retrieval shows exactly which unit text went in. Second, a fixed JSON shape lets me validate every field. Third, teacher approval keeps the exam decision with a human. Each step is small and testable, which matters for official questions.
entries.followup_en: If retrieval is empty, I stop. I do not let the model fill gaps from memory. If JSON fails Pydantic, I retry or send it to review, I do not save a broken record. Logs show the retrieved chunks, the raw model text, and who approved. In an exam bank that trail is the point. Speed is not the point.
entries.answer_ar: تقسيم الخطوات حتى يمكن فحص المصدر والشكل والموافقة. السؤال الرسمي لا يُحفظ من رد حر للنموذج.

entries.answer_en: Students can copy and change the words, so exact matching misses that. I turn assignments into embeddings and compare meaning. I split the text into chunks, because one vector for a whole paper hides a copied paragraph. The tool flags two close passages, and the teacher decides.
entries.followup_en: Each chunk has metadata: school, subject, term, assignment number. I filter on that before comparing, so I am not mixing the wrong sets. I tuned the cutoff on real teacher-reviewed pairs. This is not an LLM and not RAG. There is no generation step. A local vector store holds id, vector, text, and metadata. Chroma was a prototype evaluation only.
entries.answer_ar: المدقق يحوّل الواجب إلى متجهات ويقارن المعنى على مستوى فقرات. يُظهر التشابه للمعلم، ولا يحكم على الطالب.

entries.answer_en: Python, a sentence-embedding model from Hugging Face, and cosine similarity. I stored vectors in a lightweight local store. I tried Chroma for a prototype. I did not use an LLM here. The rest is text extraction, chunking, metadata filters, and a teacher review screen.
entries.followup_en: I would pick Qdrant or pgvector for a heavier production store, because filtering, backup, and on-premise ops matter. I have not run Qdrant in production. I know how collections and payload filters work. Pinecone is a poor fit if data must stay inside the country. No LangChain in this project. No agent.
entries.answer_ar: التقنية: بايثون وembeddings وتشابه جيب التمام وتخزين محلي خفيف. كروما للتجربة فقط، بلا نموذج لغوي.

aliases: how did you choose the similarity threshold

entries.answer_en: I did not pick a textbook number. Teachers had already reviewed some pairs: real follow-up cases, and expected overlap like shared question text. I tried different cutoffs and looked at misses and false alarms. Too low and teachers ignore the tool; too high and we miss copies, so they still decide.
entries.followup_en: Shared assignment instructions score high even when the student work is honest. Metadata filters reduce that noise before the score. I cared more about a list teachers would actually open than about a pretty chart. The cutoff can move by subject if needed. I would not freeze one global number forever.
entries.answer_ar: الحدّ اختُبر على حالات راجعها المعلمون. المنخفض يزعجهم، والمرتفع يُفلت النسخ. القرار النهائي يبقى للمعلم.

entries.answer_en: No, it is vector search and comparison: embeddings, similarity, and metadata filters. Those blocks also appear in RAG. It becomes RAG when a language model writes from the retrieved text. We did not do that; the teacher reads the two passages.
entries.followup_en: An LLM summary of the match would start to look like RAG. We avoided that because the case is about a student. I wanted the evidence on screen, not a generated accusation. Retrieval without generation is still useful. I keep the names clean so the interview and the architecture stay honest.
entries.answer_ar: ليس RAG. هو بحث متجهات ومقارنة بلا توليد. RAG يبدأ عندما يكتب النموذج من النصوص المسترجعة.

aliases: what challenges did you face in the similarity checker

entries.answer_en: Long papers were a problem, because one vector per assignment hid a copied paragraph, so I moved to chunks. Shared question text also looks similar even when work is honest, so filters and a tuned cutoff helped. Trust was the last issue: if the tool accuses students, teachers walk away.
entries.followup_en: I show the two passages side by side with the score. I never write a guilt label. Arabic and English mix in some assignments, which makes naive word matching worse and is another reason embeddings helped. I also had to extract text cleanly from messy files before any vector was computed. Garbage in still beats a fancy model.
entries.answer_ar: الصعوبة في المستندات الطويلة والإنذارات الكاذبة من نص السؤال المشترك، والثقة: الأداة تُظهر الدليل ولا تتهم.

entries.answer_en: It was a project at Al Najat Schools. We analyzed grades and attendance to identify students who might need academic support. I used Python, Pandas, and Scikit-learn. I built a classification model that flagged at-risk students so teachers could intervene early.
entries.followup_en: I kept student IDs as text so leading zeros were not lost. Missing attendance was a signal, so I added a missing flag instead of filling the average. Scaling sat inside a sklearn pipeline to avoid leakage. I respected time: the model only saw features available at that point in the term, not final grades. Most students were fine, so Accuracy would have lied.
entries.answer_ar: كان مشروعًا في مدارس Al Najat. حللنا الدرجات والحضور لتحديد الطلاب الذين قد يحتاجون دعمًا أكاديميًا. استخدمت Python و Pandas و Scikit-learn. بنيت نموذج تصنيف يحدد الطلاب المعرضين للخطر حتى يتمكن المعلمون من التدخل مبكرًا.

entries.answer_en: Recall on the students who needed support. Most students were fine, so Accuracy looks high even if you miss the ones who matter. Missing a struggling student is worse than one extra follow-up. I still watched Precision so the list did not flood teachers.
entries.followup_en: I looked at errors per class, not only the average. A confusion matrix tells you if you are only good at the majority class. If Precision collapsed, teachers would ignore the list and the whole tool would fail. The metric has to match the cost in the school, not a Kaggle leaderboard.
entries.answer_ar: المعيار الاستدعاء لأن معظم الطلاب بخير، والدقة العامة تخدع. إغفال طالب أخطر من متابعة زائدة.

entries.answer_en: Scaling lived inside a sklearn pipeline, so it fitted on training data only. Time also mattered. I was predicting early in the term, so the model could not see final grades. A random split would have leaked the future. I split in time order.
entries.followup_en: A missing-attendance flag is fine. Filling missing values with the global mean before the split is not. Any column that only exists after the outcome is known has to stay out. I treated IDs as text, not numbers, which is not leakage but it is the same careful data handling. If a score looks too good, I assume leakage first.
entries.answer_ar: منع التسريب بوضع التحويل داخل Pipeline، وبالتقسيم حسب الزمن حتى لا يرى النموذج درجات نهاية الفصل.

entries.answer_en: Helpdesk tickets arrived as free text and people routed them by hand. I trained a sklearn classifier on TF-IDF to predict the department, like accounts or network, using tickets staff had already routed. Unclear tickets went to a person, with no LLM. Faster routing, plus simple stats for reporting.
entries.followup_en: I cleaned duplicates and sensitive details first. I split train and test before learning the text features, so IDF could not peek at the test set. Ambiguous tickets were a review category, not a forced high-confidence label. If two problems sat in one ticket, forcing one department would have been worse than asking a human.
entries.answer_ar: تصنيف تذاكر الدعم بنصوص حرة باستخدام TF-IDF وsklearn. التذكرة الغامضة تذهب لشخص، بلا نموذج لغوي.
